clue.text: Cowardly soldier, but rarely without a pistol, we're told

definitions.text: Cowardly soldier, but rarely without a pistol, we're told

parts.words: Cowardly soldier, but rarely without a pistol, we're told
parts.note: a braggart rogue in Shakespeare's history plays, a crony who is seldom seen apart from his fellow swaggerer Pistol

explanation.surface: A timid trooper who, so they say, almost always carries a handgun.
explanation.walkthrough: The pistol is really Pistol, the boastful companion who shares the tavern scenes with this red-nosed corporal in Henry IV, Henry V and The Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's red-nosed corporal is a thief and a coward who runs with Pistol and Nym.

clue.text: Mary McCarthy described its wooded areas

definitions.text: Mary McCarthy described its wooded areas

parts.words: Mary McCarthy described its wooded areas
parts.note: alludes to the title of Mary McCarthy's 1952 campus satire, The Groves of ..., where groves are the wooded areas

explanation.surface: An American novelist wrote about some patches of woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: The wooded areas are the groves of McCarthy's title; the phrase itself goes back to Horace's groves of the Athenian school.
explanation.definitionFit: The academic world is called after Plato's school, held in a grove; McCarthy's novel satirises a college.

clue.text: His best-known work may be seen as old hat

definitions.text: His best-known work may be seen as old hat

parts.words: His best-known work may be seen as old hat
parts.note: the writer's most famous novel, Trilby, shares its name with a soft felt hat that took its name from the book

explanation.surface: A writer whose most famous book now seems outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like a sneer meaning out of date, but it is literal: the trilby hat is named after George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby.
explanation.definitionFit: George, grandfather of Daphne, wrote the novel Trilby, from which the felt hat got its name.

clue.text: On its own, like Waugh's unicorn

definitions.meaning: an allusion to a solitary unicorn in Evelyn Waugh, a creature with no mate

explanation.surface: Alone, like a mythical beast in an English novelist's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on your own means being solitary, and Waugh's unicorn is pictured as a creature without a companion.

clue.text: "She is like a character out of ————- the very nicest character " (Iris Murdoch)

definitions.text: "She is like a character out of ————- the very nicest character " (Iris Murdoch)

parts.words: "She is like a character out of ————- the very nicest character " (Iris Murdoch)
parts.note: a quotation from Iris Murdoch's novel Under the Net with the name of a Dutch painter of grotesque visions left blank

explanation.surface: A quotation from Iris Murdoch comparing a woman to a figure from a painter's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is filled by the painter's name, so the quotation itself serves as the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Netherlandish master of The Garden of Earthly Delights painted crowds of odd figures, any of which could be called a character.

clue.text: Artist with a missing playwright

indicators.note: missing means the word for an artist is going without the letter a that the clue names

parts.note: a painter is an artist

explanation.surface: A painter teamed up with a dramatist who has disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing' looks as if it describes the playwright, but it tells you to drop A from PAINTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter wrote The Birthday Party and The Caretaker, so he is a dramatist.

clue.text: Whose progress led to Vanity Fair?

definitions.text: Whose progress led to Vanity Fair?

parts.words: Whose progress led to Vanity Fair?
parts.note: in Bunyan's allegory the travellers on the way to the Celestial City pass through the town of Vanity, with its fair

explanation.surface: A question about whose career ended at a famous novel or magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Vanity Fair suggests Thackeray or the magazine, but it began as a fair in Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, which Christian and Faithful pass through.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunyan's travellers to the Celestial City are devout wayfarers, and their journey takes them through the town of Vanity.

clue.text: Start in Italian violin works to reveal composer

indicators.note: to reveal says the letters run inside these words and are uncovered when the string is read across them

explanation.surface: Beginning an Italian violin piece shows who wrote it.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run through 'Start in Italian'; 'violin works' is surface colour pointing at a violinist-composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Tartini was an eighteenth-century Italian violinist who wrote the Devil's Trill sonata.

clue.text: A legacy of Euphues, lodged, so to speak, in Shakespeare's memory

definitions.text: A legacy of Euphues, lodged, so to speak, in Shakespeare's memory

parts.words: A legacy of Euphues, lodged, so to speak, in Shakespeare's memory
parts.note: Thomas Lodge's romance was subtitled Euphues' Golden Legacy and was the source Shakespeare used for As You Like It

explanation.surface: Something left by a literary character, stored away in Shakespeare's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodged' puns on Thomas Lodge, the author; Shakespeare remembered his romance when writing As You Like It, whose heroine is Rosalind.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodge's 1590 prose romance, subtitled Euphues' Golden Legacy, gave Shakespeare the plot of As You Like It.

clue.text: Hauliers in Blok verse, or opera?

definitions.meaning: people who drive vehicles carrying goods, read as two words
the name of a cycle of poems by Alexander Blok, and of Bizet's opera

explanation.surface: A question whether some lorry drivers appear in a Russian poem or an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Carters who drive vans are car men; Blok's poem cycle and Bizet's opera share the gypsy heroine's name.

clue.text: Some Latin from the books

definitions.meaning: a phrase in the Latin language
the literal translation, as written on a bookplate naming a library's owner

explanation.surface: A bit of Latin taken from a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The bookplate phrase is Latin, and it translates literally as out of the library of someone.

clue.text: Unfortunately gaoled US composer

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so these letters land in a new and unlucky order

explanation.surface: An American musician has, sadly, been locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' rearranges GAOLEDUS; Gesualdo, the Renaissance prince, fittingly killed his wife and her lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlo Gesualdo, Prince of Venosa, wrote strikingly chromatic madrigals.

clue.text: "Dungeons and thrones which the same hour ——'d" (Childe Harold)

definitions.text: "Dungeons and thrones which the same hour ——'d" (Childe Harold)

parts.words: "Dungeons and thrones which the same hour ——'d" (Childe Harold)
parts.note: a line from Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, on the Doge's Palace in Venice, with the verb meaning filled again left blank

explanation.surface: A gap-fill quotation from Byron's long poem about Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's line runs 'Dungeons and thrones which the same hour refill'd', meaning prisoners and rulers replaced one another.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill a place again, as the Venetian prisons and thrones were restocked, is the verb missing from Byron's line.

clue.text: Threat from Jessie Fothergill

definitions.meaning: the title of an 1884 novel by the Victorian Lancashire novelist Jessie Fothergill

explanation.surface: A menace coming from a Victorian woman novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Danger is a threat, and Fothergill, author of The First Violin, also published a novel under that title.

clue.text: Journal to support cheaper book

parts.note: a journal is a newspaper
to back is to support

explanation.surface: A periodical backs a lower-priced volume.
explanation.definitionFit: A softcover edition costs less than a hardback.

clue.text: Cypriot king, very fond of his own work

definitions.text: Cypriot king, very fond of his own work

parts.words: Cypriot king, very fond of his own work
parts.note: in Ovid's Metamorphoses a sculptor king of Cyprus falls in love with the ivory statue he has carved

explanation.surface: A monarch from Cyprus who admires what he has made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very fond' understates it: he fell in love with his statue, which Venus brought to life; Shaw borrowed the name for his play.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid's sculptor-king of Cyprus loved his statue of Galatea, later the basis of Shaw's play.

clue.text: Not a weighty reason, we hear, for repeating an idea

indicators.note: we hear asks the solver to say the phrase out loud and find a word with the same sound

parts.note: not weighty means light, and a reason is a motive

explanation.surface: A flimsy reason, so we're told, for saying the same thing again.
explanation.walkthrough: Said out loud, 'light motive' sounds like the German musical term.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's term for a musical theme that recurs to mark a character or idea.

clue.text: Designation of unpronounceable play

parts.note: actors' superstition forbids saying the title of Macbeth in a theatre, so they call it by another name

explanation.surface: The name given to a drama that cannot be spoken aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre people refuse to name Macbeth backstage for luck, and call it 'the ... play' instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors avoid Macbeth's title and use this adjective, naming its setting north of the border, as a substitute.

clue.text: His wounds roused Achilles' drowsy blood

definitions.text: His wounds roused Achilles' drowsy blood

parts.words: His wounds roused Achilles' drowsy blood
parts.note: in the Iliad the death of Achilles' dearest friend at Hector's hands drives the sulking hero back into battle

explanation.surface: Someone's injuries woke the sluggish Greek hero to action.
explanation.walkthrough: The wording echoes Troilus and Cressida, where Achilles' sloth is ended by his friend's death.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles' companion was killed by Hector wearing his armour, and grief brought Achilles back to fight.

clue.text: Top drawer vocation for I in Windsor

definitions.text: Top drawer vocation for I in Windsor

parts.words: Top drawer vocation for I in Windsor
parts.note: in The Merry Wives of Windsor the clue's I, read as entry 1, is taken on by the Host to draw and tap beer

explanation.surface: An upper-class job for someone in a royal town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' stands for 1 across, Bardolph, who in Merry Wives becomes the Host's beer-drawer; 'top drawer' means a fine drawer of drinks, not posh.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub servant who draws beer from the cask is the job Falstaff finds for Bardolph at the Garter Inn.

clue.text: Fielding's thief-taker with English dramatist

parts.note: Jonathan Wild, the criminal thief-taker of Henry Fielding's satire

explanation.surface: A novelist's crook teams up with an English playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde wrote The Importance of Being Earnest and other comedies.

clue.text: Noble calling of Nijinsky

parts.note: Nijinsky was a male ballet star, and the leading male role-type is the '... noble'

explanation.surface: A Russian dancer's honourable profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noble calling' looks like praise of his work, but 'noble' completes the ballet term for a principal male classical dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: A male ballet dancer was Nijinsky's profession; the top classical rank is called noble.

clue.text: Novelist associated with James branch

parts.note: the American fantasy writer whose full name joins James and Branch before his surname

explanation.surface: A writer linked to a branch of the James family.
explanation.walkthrough: James Branch is not a family line but the given names of the Virginian author of Jurgen.
explanation.definitionFit: James Branch Cabell wrote Jurgen and other fantasy novels set in imaginary Poictesme.

clue.text: Hope inspired game and impudent villain

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
pert means impudent or cheeky

explanation.surface: A novelist inspired a game and a cheeky rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope inspired' refers to Anthony Hope, whose The Prisoner of Zenda has the villain Rupert of Hentzau.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert of Hentzau is the scheming antagonist in Anthony Hope's Ruritanian romance.

clue.text: Handsome French upland writer whose collaborator was in arms manufacture?

definitions.text: writer whose collaborator was in arms manufacture?

parts.note: beau is French for handsome
mont is French for a mountain, upland country

explanation.surface: A good-looking French hill man's partner made weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: His partner was Fletcher, and a fletcher makes arrows, hence arms manufacture.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Beaumont co-wrote Jacobean plays with John Fletcher, whose surname is the old word for an arrow-maker.

clue.text: Marcus, silver-tongued triumvir

parts.note: the Roman orator and general who formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus

explanation.surface: A Roman named Marcus, eloquent member of a ruling trio.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony's Latin name; his funeral oration for Caesar in Shakespeare is the silver tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony, Marcus by first name, was a famous orator and one of the three men of the Second Triumvirate.

clue.text: Miss Dudley, among the brightest heroines of Henry Adams

indicators.note: among says the name sits inside the run of letters across these two words

parts.words: the brightest heroines of Henry Adams

explanation.surface: A young woman who is one of an American writer's cleverest heroines.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across 'brightest heroines'; the rest of that phrase is cover, pointing to the painter heroine of Henry Adams's 1884 novel, named for her.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Adams's 1884 novel is named for its heroine, a young painter surnamed Dudley.

clue.text: The kir -mixed from Moore's brook?

indicators.note: mixed suggests a cocktail being stirred, so the letters are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A white-wine cocktail stirred from a stream's water.
explanation.walkthrough: George Moore's novel The Brook Kerith retells the Gospel; 'mixed' rearranges THEKIR.
explanation.definitionFit: George Moore's novel takes its title from the biblical brook Cherith, spelt Kerith.

clue.text: Club where the Mad Monks discussed burning issues under

definitions.text: Club where the Mad Monks discussed burning issues under

parts.words: Club where the Mad Monks discussed burning issues under
parts.note: Sir Francis Dashwood's eighteenth-century society, nicknamed the Monks of Medmenham, met in caves and was named after damnation's flames

explanation.surface: A society of crazy friars debated urgent matters below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burning issues' looks like hot topics but points to the flames of damnation in the club's name; it met in caves at West Wycombe.
explanation.definitionFit: Dashwood's Georgian rakes' society was named after the flames of the damned.
